Irene—thanks for taking this on. A few constraints from our infra/security teams: 
- All inbound IPs must be in a short, static allowlist (we cannot accept large IP ranges).
- No inbound NAT is allowed; we must preserve source IPs for downstream firewalls.
- Our on-prem firewall is strict: MTU reductions are applied for VPN tunnels which has caused broken fragments in the past.

We are evaluating two approaches: (A) a PrivateLink-style model where we call into vendor-managed endpoints from our VPCs, or (B) a peering/transit approach where we peer with your VPC and traffic flows directly. VPN is the fallback but brings latency/MTU concerns. Can Redwood propose a hybrid that gives us static egress and predictable service IPs?

Attached is our rough network diagram (network-diagram-acme.png) and the allowlist template. Happy to run a quick call today.

Thanks Alex — appreciate the clear constraints. High level suggestion from our side: propose a split-plane model to balance security, source-IP fidelity, and operational simplicity:

1) Control plane (API calls, model selection, auth): expose via AWS PrivateLink endpoints (interface ENIs) that are single-IP-per-AZ and can be included in your allowlist. PrivateLink keeps the control traffic inside Acme's VPC-to-Redwood-hosted endpoint; no cross-account routing required back to your on-prem.

2) Data plane (high-throughput token streams): for low-latency, preserve-source-ip and egress expectations we recommend cross-account VPC peering or Transit Gateway peering for high-throughput customers (peering when limited accounts; TGW if multi-account scale). This avoids VPN MTU fragmentation and preserves path transparency.

3) Fallback / regulated traffic: for environments that require strict egress via on-prem firewalls (or where peering is prohibited), we offer an S2S VPN tunnel option with MSS/MTU tuning and TCP MSS clamping. Use VPN only where PrivateLink + peering are impossible.

I'll put together a short pros/cons matrix and a recommended diagram with IP allocations. Can you confirm whether Acme prefers single-AZ allowlist IPs or an IP range per AZ? That will shape which option we push.

Next steps: I'll loop in product networking for cost estimates (Ben) and the infra architect for Transit Gateway notes (Marcus).

—Irene

Quick technical notes that matter for design decisions:
- PrivateLink provides per-AZ interface endpoints with stable ENI IPs in the caller VPC. Good for allowlist. The downside is that data sent over PrivateLink flows through our NLBs and may incur slightly higher latency and per-GB data charges.
- VPC peering preserves source IPs fully — but does not support transitive routing. If Acme uses multiple AWS accounts, we need either multiple peering connections or Transit Gateway. TGW introduces an additional recurring cost but simplifies many-to-many routing and supports route propagation.
- Site-to-site VPN: avoid for token heavy workloads because of MTU and throughput constraints (we've seen up to 30-40% perf drop at high QPS through common tunnels). If needed, we recommend AES-GCM and MTU tuning plus TCP MSS clamp at the customer edge.
- Observability: with peering we can pass trace headers and use existing eBPF flow collectors on the Acme side; PrivateLink hides some of the intermediate hops behind the interface endpoint so you'll need edge-level tracing.

I'll attach a short table in the next message with ballpark monthly cost delta (data + hourly endpoint/peering cost) for comparison.

—Kimberly

Attached is the short cost sketch and two recommended templates. TL;DR cost comparison for expected pilot traffic (20M tokens/day, ~1TB/mo egress):
- PrivateLink-only (control + data over PrivateLink): estimated incremental data transfer + endpoint charges ~ $3,200/mo (higher per-GB and endpoint hourly).
- Peering (control via PrivateLink, data over peering/TGW): estimated ~$1,100/mo (peering interregional costs and TGW hourly if used).
- S2S VPN fallback (data over VPN): ~$900/mo but with perf caveats — throughput throttling, higher SRE load for fragmentation issues.

Recommendation: Start with hybrid: PrivateLink for control plane (allowlist-friendly) + peering for the data plane (single-account peering or TGW if you need cross-account). Keep S2S as a formally documented fallback with MTU guidance.
